title: You’ve saved enough to enjoy some of it
summary: Why the number you're waiting to hit before you "relax" almost never stays put What Canada's own consumer watchdog says financial well-being actually includes, and it isn't just a bigger balance A short test you can run this week to see if you're already funded enough to loosen your grip a little
body_markdown:
## Highlights


- Why the number you're waiting to hit before you "relax" almost never stays put
- What Canada's own consumer watchdog says financial well-being actually includes, and it isn't just a bigger balance
- A short test you can run this week to see if you're already funded enough to loosen your grip a little


You did the hard part - built the emergency fund, automated the RRSP contribution, hit the milestone you set two years ago. The system works. But if you're the kind of person who's good at saving and investing, actually spending some of what you built can feel strangely uncomfortable.


Here are ways to start enjoying what you’ve created.


## When "not yet" becomes permanent


Good financial habits often start as protection.


The trouble is those habits can work so well that they stop being a phase and start being an identity. The goalpost keeps moving. "I'll relax at $100,000." Then $250,000. Then the mortgage gets a little smaller, and retirement gets a little more funded, and the target resets again.[One Passiv user tracking her progress toward a million dollars in investments](https://passiv.com/blog/how-i-m-saving-for-retirement-in-3-years-we-ll-have-a-million-in-investments) put it simply: the next milestone is already on the calendar before the last one has really sunk in.


There's nothing wrong with discipline. The problem shows up when future-you gets every benefit of the plan and present-you never gets a turn.


## Enjoying your money is part of being financially well, not the opposite of it


It's easy to treat "enjoy your money" and "be responsible with your money" as opposites.[Canada's Financial Consumer Agency](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/programs/research/financial-well-being-survey-results.html) doesn't see it that way. Its definition of financial well-being goes beyond income: it includes meeting your current needs, having the resilience to absorb a setback, staying on track for your goals, and, in the agency's own words, having the financial freedom to make choices that allow you to enjoy life.


In other words, enjoyment isn't the thing your financial plan is protecting you from. It can be one of the outcomes the plan was built to produce. The useful question isn't "have I saved enough." It's this: *what has your financial progress already made possible that you're still not letting yourself use?*


## Spend on what actually changes your days


Enjoying your money doesn't have to mean a big purchase or abandoning your long-term plan. Look for spending that changes how your actual days feel.


**Buy back time.**[A 2017 study of more than 6,000 adults across the US, Canada, Denmark, and the Netherlands](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5559044/) found that people who spend money on time-saving services report greater life satisfaction, and working adults report greater happiness after a time-saving purchase than after a material one. That could mean grocery delivery during a chaotic month, someone to clean every other week, or finally paying for the direct flight instead of the layover.


**Spend on what you actually value** , not what a financially successful person is supposed to enjoy. A weekend away, a class you've been thinking about for years, dinner with friends. You get to decide what matters most to you.


**Remove a recurring source of friction.** The subscription that annoys you every renewal. The commute that eats an hour a day. Small, ongoing frustrations are often cheaper to fix than they feel.


**Be generous, if that's what matters to you.** Help a family member, give a real gift, host the people you care about. Money creates value beyond your own balance sheet too.


## Build permission into the system, not into willpower


If spending makes you anxious, waiting to magically feel relaxed about it doesn't work. A better fix is a rule, so you're not making the decision fresh every time.


Start with the floor: know your bills, your buffer, and the saving and investing level your plan actually needs. Then decide what "enough for now" looks like. Not a permanent finish line, just a checkpoint that says the plan is funded well enough that you don't need to squeeze every spare dollar out of this month.


From there, assign a guilt-free amount a job. If the long-term plan is already funded, spending the money set aside for enjoyment isn't breaking the plan. It's following it. Some people go further and set enjoyment goals alongside savings goals: two Fridays off this summer, a trip to see a sibling, finally booking the course.


## Don't turn enjoying money into another project


High-achievers can turn even leisure into a performance metric, hunting for the mathematically optimal vacation or the "best" way to spend $200.[Research on spending and happiness](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11659422/) suggests there isn't one universally "best" way to spend money; different kinds of purchases make people happy for different reasons.


A more useful habit is noticing the result after you spend, rather than optimizing before. The slower Saturday. The dinner you didn't have to cook. The trip you'll still remember in five years. If you already hit a milestone worth marking, it's worth actually[noticing the ones you've already reached](https://passiv.com/blog/7-milestones-that-prove-your-investments-are-on-the-right-track/) instead of only looking at the next one.


## Let the system give some time back


A mature financial system shouldn't need constant tinkering. Automate what's repetitive. Review on a schedule instead of every time the market moves. Use a clear target so most decisions are already made before they come up.


The point of building a system was never only to grow the number. It was also to shrink how much mental space the portfolio takes up.[One Passiv user described it](https://passiv.com/blog/9-ways-passiv-helps-me-build-wealth/) as the difference between fiddling with spreadsheets every month and letting the system do the math for her.


## You don't have to stop investing to start enjoying it


None of this means stop saving, stop investing, or suddenly become a big spender. It means noticing that some of the future you were preparing for may already be here. Financial security matters because of what it lets you do, not only because of what the number says.


Keep the plan. Keep investing. But let it buy you some time, comfort, connection, and enjoyment along the way, not just a bigger balance to check.
